From the Division of the Kingdom to the Ascent of the Throne by Ahab in the 38th Year of Asa King of Judah - 1 Kings 12-16:28 <div eID="gen4926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4927" type="x-p"/> This epoch embraces only fifty-seven years, which are filled up in the kingdom of Judah by the reigns of three kings, and in the kingdom of Israel by six rulers from four different houses, Jeroboam’s sin of rebellion against the ordinance and commandment of God having produced repeated rebellions, so that one dynasty was ever rising up to overthrow and exterminate another. - Commencing with the secession of the ten tribes from Rehoboam, we have first of all an account of the founding of the kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 12), and of the predictions of the prophets concerning the introduction of the calf-worship (1 Kings 13) and the rejection of Jeroboam and his house by God (1 Kings 14:1-20); and after this the most important facts connected with the reigns of Rehoboam, Abijam, and Asa are given (1 Kings 14:21-15:24); and, finally, a brief history of the kingdom of Israel from the ascent of the throne by Nadab to the death of Omri (1 Kings 15:25-16:28). <div eID="gen4927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4928" type="x-p"/> 1Ki 12:1-24 <div eID="gen4928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4929" type="x-p"/> The jealousy which had prevailed from time immemorial between Ephraim and Judah, the two most powerful tribes of the covenant nation, and had broken out on different occasions into open hostilities (Jdg 8:1.; <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.9">2Sa 2:9</reference>; 2Sa 19:42.), issued, on the death of Solomon, in the division of the kingdom; ten tribes, headed by Ephraim, refusing to do homage to Rehoboam, the son and successor of Solomon, and choosing Jeroboam the Ephraimite as their king. Now, although the secession of the ten tribes from the royal house of David had been ordained by God as a punishment for Solomon’s idolatry, and not only had Solomon been threatened with this punishment, but the sovereignty over ten tribes had been promised to Jeroboam by the prophet Ahijah, whilst the secession itself was occasioned by Rehoboam’s imprudence; yet it was essentially a rebellion against the Lord and His anointed, a conspiracy on the part of these tribes against Judah and its king Rehoboam. For apart from the fact that the tribes had no right to choose at their pleasure a different king from the one who was the lawful heir to the throne of David, the very circumstance that the tribes who were discontented with Solomon’s government did not come to Jerusalem to do homage to Rehoboam, but chose Sichem as the place of meeting, and had also sent for Jeroboam out of Egypt, showed clearly enough that it was their intention to sever themselves from the royal house of David; so that the harsh reply given by Rehoboam to their petition that the service imposed upon them might be lightened, furnished them with the desired opportunity for carrying out the secession upon which they had already resolved, and for which Jeroboam was the suitable man. And we have already shown at 1Ki 11:40 that the promise of the throne, which Jeroboam had already received from God, neither warranted him in rebelling against Solomon, nor in wresting to himself the government over the tribes that were discontented with the house of David after Solomon’s death. The usurpation of the throne was therefore Jeroboam’s first sin (vv. 1-24), to which he added a second and much greater one immediately after his ascent of the throne, namely, the establishment of an unlawful worship, by which he turned the political division into a religious schism and a falling away from Jehovah the God-King of His people (1Ki 12:25-33). <div eID="gen4929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4930" type="x-p"/> 1Ki 12:1 <div eID="gen4930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4931" type="x-p"/> Secession of the Ten Tribes (cf., 2 Chron 10:1-11:4). - 1Ki 12:1-4. Rehoboam went to Shechem, because all Israel had come thither to make him king. “All Israel,” according to what follows (cf., 1Ki 12:20, 1Ki 12:21), was the ten tribes beside Judah and Benjamin. The right of making king the prince whom God had chosen, i.e., of anointing him and doing homage to him (compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.38">1Ch 12:38</reference>, where המליך alternates with למלך משׁך,   (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.4">2Sa 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.3">2Sa 5:3</reference>), was an old traditional right in Israel, and the tribes had exercised it not only in the case of Saul and David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.15">1Sa 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.4">2Sa 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.3">2Sa 5:3</reference>), but in that of Solomon also (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.22">1Ch 29:22</reference>). The ten tribes of Israel made use of this right on Rehoboam’s ascent of the throne; but instead of coming to Jerusalem, the residence of the king and capital of the kingdom, as they ought to have done, and doing homage there to the legitimate successor of Solomon, they had gone to Sichem, the present Nabulus (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.33.18">Gen 33:18</reference>), the place where the ancient national gatherings were held in the tribe of Ephraim (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.1">Jos 24:1</reference>), and where Abimelech the son of Gideon had offered himself as king in the time of the Judges (Jdg 9:1.). On the choice of Sichem as the place for doing homage Kimchi has quite correctly observed, that “they sought an opportunity for transferring the government to Jeroboam, and therefore were unwilling to come to Jerusalem, but came to Sichem, which belonged to Ephraim, whilst Jeroboam was an Ephraimite.” If there could be any further doubt on the matter, it would be removed by the fact that they had sent for Jeroboam the son of Nebat to come from Egypt, whither he had fled from Solomon (1Ki 11:40), and attend this meeting, and that Jeroboam took the lead in the meeting, and no doubt suggested to those assembled the demand which they should lay before Rehoboam (1Ki 12:4).<note placement="foot">“This pretext was no doubt furnished to the people by Jeroboam, who, because he had formerly been placed above Ephraim as superintendent of the works, could most craftily suggest calumnies, from the things which he knew better than others.” - (Seb. Schmidt.</note>
entries.779022fa0f5eb5bc8f87e077b80bb75969140e94: 1Ki 12:25 <div eID="gen4943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4944" type="x-p"/> Founding of the Kingdom of Israel. - 1Ki 12:25. When Jeroboam had become king, it was his first care to give a firmer basis to his sovereignty by the fortification of Sichem and Pnuel. בּנח, to build, is used here in the sense of fortifying, because both cities had stood for a long time, and nothing is known of their having been destroyed under either Solomon or David, although the tower of Sichem had been burnt down by Abimelech (Jdg 9:49), and the tower of Pnuel had been destroyed by Gideon (Jdg 8:17). <hi type="italic">Sichem</hi>, a place well known from the time of Abraham downwards (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.6">Gen 12:6</reference>), was situated upon the mountains of Ephraim, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and still exists under the name of <hi type="italic">Nabulus</hi> or <hi type="italic">Nablûs</hi>, a name corrupted from <hi type="italic">Flavia Neapolis</hi>. Jeroboam dwelt therein, i.e., he chose it at first as his residence, though he afterwards resided in Thirza (see 1Ki 14:17). <hi type="italic">Pnuel</hi> was situated, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.32.31">Gen 32:31</reference>, on the other side of the Jordan, on the northern bank of the Jabbok (not the southern side, as Thenius supposes); and judging from Gen 32:22. and Jdg 8:8., it was on the caravan road, which led through Gilead to Damascus, and thence past Palmyra and along the Euphrates to Mesopotamia. It was probably on account of its situation that Jeroboam fortified it, to defend his sovereignty over Gilead against hostile attacks from the north-east and east.
entries.ee9ba4d31f36531885e6f431a381a4dc0b58382e: 1Ki 12:26-27 <div eID="gen4944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4945" type="x-p"/> In order also to give internal strength to his kingdom, Jeroboam resolved to provide for his subjects a substitute for the sacrificial worship in the temple by establishing new <hi type="italic">sacra</hi>, and thus to take away all occasion for making festal journeys to Jerusalem, from which he apprehended, and that probably not without reason, a return of the people to the house of David and consequently further danger for his own life. “If this people go up to perform sacrifice in the house of Jehovah at Jerusalem, their heart will turn to their lord, king Rehoboam,” etc.
entries.3e421443246633cb630533e30d5f30dce0962615: 1Ki 12:28-29 <div eID="gen4945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4946" type="x-p"/> He therefore consulted, sc., with his counsellors, or the heads of the nation, who had helped him to the throne, and made two calves of gold. זהב עגלי are young oxen, not of pure gold however, or cast in brass and gilded, but in all probability like the golden calf which Aaron had cast for the people at Sinai, made of a kernel of wood, which was then covered with gold plate (see the Comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.32.4">Exo 32:4</reference>). That Jeroboam had in his mind not merely the Egyptian <hi type="italic">Apis</hi>-worship generally, but more especially the image-worship which Aaron introduced for the people at Sinai, is evident from the words borrowed from <reference osisRef="Exod.32.4">Exo 32:4</reference>, with which he studiously endeavoured to recommend his new form of worship to the people: “Behold, this is thy God, O Israel, who brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” רב־לכם מעלות, it is too much for you to go to Jerusalem; not “let your going suffice,” because מן is not to be taken in a partitive sense here, as it is in <reference osisRef="Exod.9.28">Exo 9:28</reference> and Eze 44:6. What Jeroboam meant to say by the words, “Behold thy God,” etc., was, “this is no new religion, but this was the form of worship which our fathers used in the desert, with Aaron himself leading the way” (Seb. Schmidt). And whilst the verbal allusion to that event at Sinai plainly shows that this worship was not actual idolatry, i.e., was not a worship of Egyptian idols, from which it is constantly distinguished in our books as well as in Hosea and Amos, but that Jehovah was worshipped under the image of the calves or young oxen; the choice of the places in which the golden calves were set up also shows that Jeroboam desired to adhere as closely as possible to ancient traditions. He did not select his own place of residence, but Bethel and Dan. <hi type="italic">Bethel</hi>, on the southern border of his kingdom, which properly belonged to the tribe of Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.13">Jos 18:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.18.22">Jos 18:22</reference>), the present <hi type="italic">Beitin</hi>, had already been consecrated as a divine seat by the vision of Jehovah which the patriarch Jacob received there in a dream (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.11">Gen 28:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.19">Gen 28:19</reference>), and Jacob gave it the name of <hi type="italic">Bethel</hi>, house of God, and afterwards built an altar there to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.7">Gen 35:7</reference>). And Jeroboam may easily have fancied, and have tried to persuade others, that Jehovah would reveal Himself to the descendants of Jacob in this sacred place just as well as He had done to their forefather. - <hi type="italic">Dan</hi>, in the northern part of the kingdom, on the one source of the Jordan, formerly called <hi type="italic">Laish</hi> (Jdg 18:26.), was also consecrated as a place of worship by the image-worship established there by the Danites, at which even a grandson of Moses had officiated; and regard may also have been had to the convenience of the people, namely, that the tribes living in the north would not have to go a long distance to perform their worship.
entries.556b8d75dd90fd0641e991b24beb561c5dd68190: 1Ki 12:30-31 <div eID="gen4946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4947" type="x-p"/> But this institution became a sin to Jeroboam, because it violated the fundamental law of the Old Testament religion, since this not only prohibited all worship of Jehovah under images and symbols (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.4">Exo 20:4</reference>), but had not even left the choice of the place of worship to the people themselves (Deu 12:5.). “And the people went before the one to Dan.” The expression “to Dan” can only be suitably explained by connecting it with העם: the people even to Dan, i.e., the people throughout the whole kingdom even to Dan. The southern boundary as the <hi type="italic">terminus a quo</hi> is not mentioned; not because it was for a long time in dispute, but because it was already given in the allusion to Bethel. האחד is neither the golden calf at Dan nor (as I formerly thought) that at Bethel, but is to be interpreted according to the receding את־האחד ואת־האחד: one of the two, or actually both the one and the other (Thenius). The sin of which Jeroboam was guilty consisted in the fact that he no longer allowed the people to go to the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, but induced or compelled them to worship Jehovah before one or the other of the calves which he had set up, or  (as it is expressed in 1Ki 12:31) made a house of high places, בּמות בּית (see at 1Ki 3:2), instead of the house of God, which the Lord had sanctified as the place of worship by filling it with His gracious presence. The singular בּית ב may be accounted for from the antithesis to יהוה בּית, upon which it rests. There was no necessity to say expressly that there was a house of high places at Bethel and Dan, i.e., in two places, because it followed as a matter of course that the golden calves could not stand in the open air, but were placed in a temple, by which the sacrificial altar stood. These places of worship were houses of <hi type="italic">high places</hi>, <hi type="italic">Bamoth</hi>, because the ark of the covenant was wanting, and therewith the gracious presence of God, the <hi type="italic">Shechinah</hi>, for which no symbol invented by men could be a substitute. Moreover Jeroboam made “priests from the mass of the people, who were not of the sons of Levi.” העם מקצות, i.e., not of the poorest of the people (Luther and others), but from the last of the people onwards, that is to say, from the whole of the people any one without distinction even to the very last, instead of the priests chosen by God out of the tribe of Levi. For this meaning of מקצות see <reference osisRef="Gen.19.4">Gen 19:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.2">Eze 33:2</reference>, also Lud. de Dieu on this passage. This innovation on the part of Jeroboam appears very surprising, if we consider how the Ephraimite Micah (Jdg 17:10.) rejoiced that he had obtained a Levite to act as priest for his image-worship, and can only be explained from the fact that the Levites did not consent to act as priests in the worship before the golden calves, but set their faces against it, and therefore, as is stated in <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.13-2Chr.11.14">2Ch 11:13-14</reference>, were obliged to leave their district towns and possessions and emigrate into the kingdom of Judah.
entries.4bc12f002c37e09566842cf0256dcc61818b6e23: 1Ki 12:32-33 <div eID="gen4947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4948" type="x-p"/> Jeroboam also transferred to the eighth month the feast which ought to have been kept in the seventh month (the feast of tabernacles, Lev 23:34.). The pretext for this arbitrary alteration of the law, which repeatedly describes the seventh month as the month appointed by the Lord (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Lev 23:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.39">Lev 23:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.41">Lev 23:41</reference>), he may have found in the fact that in the northern portion of the kingdom the corn ripened a month later than in the more southern Judah (see my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäol</hi>. ii. §118, Anm. 3, and §119, Anm. 2), since this feast of the ingathering of the produce of the threshing-floor and wine-press (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exo 23:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.39">Lev 23:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.13">Deu 16:13</reference>) was a feast of thanksgiving for the gathering in of all the fruits of the ground. But the true reason was to be found in his intention to make the separation in a religious point of view as complete as possible, although Jeroboam retained the day of the month, the fifteenth, for the sake of the weak who took offence at his innovations. For we may see very clearly that many beside the Levites were very discontented with these illegal institutions, from the notice in <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.16">2Ch 11:16</reference>, that out of all the tribes those who were devoted to the Lord from the heart went to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the God of the fathers there. “And he sacrificed upon the altar.” This clause is connected with the preceding one, in the sense of: he instituted the feast and offered sacrifices thereat. In <hi type="italic">1Ki 12:32</hi> (from עשׂה כּן onwards) and 1Ki 12:33, what has already been related concerning Jeroboam’s religious institutions is brought to a close by a comprehensive repetition of the leading points. “Thus did he in Bethel, (namely) to offer sacrifice to the calves; and there he appointed the priests of the high places which he had made, and offered sacrifice upon the altar which he had made at Bethel, on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, which he himself had devised, and so made a feast for the children of Israel and sacrificed upon the altar to turn.” מלּבד signifies <hi type="italic">seorsum</hi>, by himself alone, i.e., in this connection, <hi type="italic">i.q</hi>. “from his own heart.” The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> מלּבּו is therefore a correct explanation as to the fact; but it is a needless correction from Neh 6:8. The last clause, להקטיר...ויּעל, leads on to what follows, and it would be more correct to take it in connection with 1Ki 13:1 and render it thus: and when he was offering sacrifice upon the altar to burn, behold there came a man of God, etc. Thenius has rendered ויּעל incorrectly, and he stood at the altar. This thought would have been expressed by הם על ויּעמוד, as in 1Ki 13:1. By הקטיר we are not to understand the burning or offering of incense, but the burning of the sacrificial portions of the flesh upon the altar, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.1.9">Lev 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.13">Lev 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.17">Lev 1:17</reference>, etc. A prophet out of Judah announces to Jeroboam the eventual overthrow of the idolatrous worship, and attests his divine mission by miraculous signs upon the altar at Bethel and the hardened king (1Ki 13:1-10); but on the way back he allows himself to be enticed by an old prophet out of Bethel to go into his house, contrary to the express command of the Lord, and while sitting at table with him has to hear from his mouth the divine threat, that on account of his transgression of the command of God he will not come into the sepulchre of his fathers. This threat was fulfilled on his way home; and the marvellous fulfilment made so deep an impression upon the old prophet, that he confirmed the testimony which he had given concerning the worship at the high places (vv. 11-32). These marvellous occurrences not only teach how Jeroboam brought about the overthrow of his dynasty by his thorough hardening against the word of God (1Ki 13:33, 1Ki 13:34), but they also show how false prophecy rose up from the very beginning in the kingdom of Israel and set itself against the true prophets of the Lord, and how it gained a victory, which merely displayed its own impotence, however, and foreshadowed its eventual and certain overthrow.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.12"/> <div eID="gen4948" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND <ns0:note place="margin">

                        </ns0:gap> C<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 10. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Rehoboam went to Shechem; for all Israel were come to Shechem <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Rehoboam</ns0:hi> did not call them thither, but went thither, because the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> prevented him, and had generally pitched upon that place, rather than upon <ns0:hi>Ierusalem;</ns0:hi> partly, because it was most convenient for all, as being in the Cen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter of the whole Kingdom: partly, because that being in the potent Tribe of <ns0:hi>Ephraim,</ns0:hi> they supposed there they might use that freedom of speech, which they resolved to use, to get their Grievances Redressed: and partly, by the secret direction of <ns0:hi>Ieroboam,</ns0:hi> or his friends, who would not trust themselves in <ns0:hi>Ierusalem;</ns0:hi> and thought <ns0:hi>Shechem</ns0:hi> a fitter place to execute their Design.</ns0:note> to make him king <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To Confirm him in the Kingdom, which they generally intended to do; he being the undoubted Heir of the Crown, and the onely Son which <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> had from so vast a number of Wives.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And it came to pass, when Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who was yet in <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 11. 4<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Egypt, heard <ns0:hi>of it</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> it is onely <ns0:hi>heard,</ns0:hi> and may relate either to <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s Death, or to the meeting which all the Tribes had appointed at <ns0:hi>Shechem.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, (for he was fled from the presence of king Solo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon, and Jeroboam dwelt in Egypt)</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 That they sent and called him <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">When the People sent him word of <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s Death, they also sent a summons for him to come to <ns0:hi>Shechem.</ns0:hi> Or, As soon as he had heard the tidings of <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s Death from others, or from common Fame; presently there came a solemn Message to him from the people, who desired his presence and assistance, as it seems probable from divers Motives; some, that they might translate the Kingdom from <ns0:hi>Rehoboam</ns0:hi> to him; and others onely for this reason, That the Presence and Countenance of a man of so great Inte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rest and Reputation, and one that had some Claim or Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tence upon the Kingdom, might lay the greater obligation upon <ns0:hi>Rehoboam</ns0:hi> to grant their desires of ease and relief.</ns0:note>: and Jero<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />boam, and all the congregation of Israel came and spake unto Rehoboam, saying,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Thy father made our <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4. 7.</ns0:note> yoke grievous <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">By heavy Taxes and Impositions, not onely for the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple and his Magnificent Buildings, but for the Expences of his Numerous Court, and of so many Wives and Concubines, whose Luxury and Idolatry must needs be very costly. And <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi> having so grosly forsaken God, it is no wonder if he Oppressed the People, and made their Yoke most grievous, as they speak. But here the Peoples perverseness is very ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servable, both in this, that they mention and aggravate one<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly the grievances of the Government, but take no notice of the vast benefits which they received from it; and in that, that they mind nothing but their outward pressures, and have no regard unto that Abominable Idolatry which he set up among them; being, it seemed, either leavened with it by his pernicious Example, or grown careless and negligent of all the concerns of Religion. By which, see how ripe they were all for those dreadful Judgments of God which are now ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stening upon them.</ns0:note>: now therefore make thou the grievous service of thy father, and his heavy yoke which he put upon us, lighter, and we will serve thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And he said unto them, Depart yet <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> three days, then come again to me <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Give me that time for deliberation and advice.</ns0:note>. And the people departed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 ¶ And king Rehoboam consulted with the old men that stood before Solomon his father <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">With <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s old Councellors, whom Age and Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perience of Men and Things, and converse with such a King, had made wise.</ns0:note>, while<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> he yet lived, and said, How do ye advise, that I may answer this people?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And they spake unto him, saying, If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">By complying with their desires, and condescending to them for a season, till the troubled humours be quieted, and the opportunity they now have, and some of them that seek for Sedition, be gone, and thou beest better stablished in thy Throne. They use this expression, as fore-seeing that some would disswade him from this course, as servile or slavish, and below the Majesty of a Prince.</ns0:note>, and wilt serve them, and <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">For, <ns0:hi>that is,</ns0:hi> Thy Service, say they, is not hard, it is onely a few good words, which it is as easie to give as bad ones.</ns0:note> answer them, and speak good words to them, then they will be thy ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 But he forsook the counsel of the old men <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Judging it unworthy of his Majesty and Authority, and likely to encourage and increase the People in their In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />solent Demands.</ns0:note>, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">So called comparatively to the Old Men; otherwise they were near 40 years old, as the following words imply.</ns0:note> that were grown up with him <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which is added as the reason of his in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clination to their Counsels, because his daily converse with them, and the likeness of their Age and Humour to his, had engaged his Affections to them, and that bribed his judgment, as it commonly doth.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> which stood before him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And he said unto them, What counsel give ye, that we may answer this people, who have
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:287" />
spoken to me, saying, Make the yoke which thy father did put upon us, lighter?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And the young men that were grown up with him, spake unto him, saying, Thus shalt thou speak unto this people that spake unto thee, saying, Thy father made our yoke heavy, but make thou <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> lighter unto us; thus shalt thou say unto them, My little <ns0:hi>finger</ns0:hi> shall be thicker <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or rather <ns0:hi>is thicker,</ns0:hi> and therefore stronger, and more able to crush you, if you proceed in these Mutinous De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mands, <ns0:hi>than his loyns,</ns0:hi> in which is the principal Seat of Strength. My father was young and weak, and had many Enemies when he first took the Kingdom; but I am the undoubted heir; and I find the Kingdom by his wise Care, far better setled and fortified against all Enemies Foreign or Domestick, than he did.</ns0:note> than my fathers loins.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And now whereas my father did lade you with an heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Make it heavier and stronger, both to punish your Petulancy, and to curb and restrain you from Seditious Attempts.</ns0:note>: my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> With such Whips as will Sting you like Scorpions: If you proceed in these courses, I will most se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verely punish you for it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 ¶ So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king had appoin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted, saying, Come to me again the third day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And the king answered the people <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> hardly.</ns0:note> rough<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly; and forsook the old mens counsel that they gave him:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And spake to them after the course of the young men, saying, My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke; my father <ns0:hi>also</ns0:hi> chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Wherefore the king hearkned not unto the people, for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Judg. 14. 4. and 2 Chron. 10. 15. and 22. 7. and 25. 20.</ns0:note> the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">Gr. the turn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing.</ns0:note> cause was from the LORD <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Who gave up <ns0:hi>Rehoboam</ns0:hi> to so foolish and fatal a mistake, and alienated the Peoples Affections from him; and ordered all Circumstances by his Wise Providence to that end.</ns0:note>, that he might perform his saying, which the LORD <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 11. 31.</ns0:note> spake by Ahijah the Shilonite, unto Jeroboam the son of Nebat.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 ¶ So when all Israel saw that the king heark<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned not unto them, the people answered the king, saying, What portion have we in David <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Family and Son; we can expect no be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nefit or relief from him, and therefore we renounce all Commerce with him, and Subjection to him. See 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 20. 1. They named <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> rather than <ns0:hi>Rehoboam;</ns0:hi> to signifie, That they did Renounce, not <ns0:hi>Rehoboam</ns0:hi> onely, but all <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Family.</ns0:note>? neither <ns0:hi>have we</ns0:hi> inheritance in the son of Jesse <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">So they call <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in contempt; q. d. <ns0:hi>Rehoboam</ns0:hi> hath no reason to carry himself with such Pride and Contempt toward his People; for if we trace his Original, it was as mean and obscure as many of ours. And since he abuseth his Power, let us reduce him to his former Obscurity.</ns0:note>: to your tents, O Israel <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Let us all forsake him, and go to our own homes, there to consider, and then to meet, and conclude how to provide otherwise for our selves.</ns0:note>; now see to thine own house, David <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Govern thy own Family; for thou shalt no longer Rule over us. Thus they brake out into Actual Rebellion against him, whom God had made their Lawful Soveraign; wherein, though they fulfilled God's Counsel, yet they Violated his Authority and Command. And they do again make an opprobrious men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> whom they should not have named without Honour.</ns0:note>. So Israel departed unto their tents.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 11. 32.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>as for</ns0:hi> the children of Israel which dwelt in the cities of Judah <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">By which Phrase he principally understands the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah;</ns0:hi> but withal, those parts and parcels of the Tribes of <ns0:hi>Levi,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Simeon,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> whose dwellings were within the Confines of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> or intermixed with them.</ns0:note>, Rehoboam reigned over them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Then king Rehoboam sent Adoram, who <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> over the tribute <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Him he sent, either 1. To pacifie the People, and pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise them Relief, now when it was too late. But then he would not have sent a person so ungrateful to the People, as that sort of men use to be. Or rather, 2. To pursue the Counsel which he had resolved upon, and to execute his Office, and, exact their Tribute with Rigor and Violence, if need were.</ns0:note>, and all Israel stoned him with stones that he died: therefore king Rehoboam <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="19">19 So Israel <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> fell away.</ns0:note> rebelled <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Their Revolt is called <ns0:hi>Rebellion,</ns0:hi> and therefore was sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful, because it was contrary to God's Authority, and Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand of subjection to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and his Seed for ever; from which the People were not freed by God's Promise and Grant made to <ns0:hi>Ieroboam,</ns0:hi> which was but a Secret Trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />action, not yet sufficiently Revealed to them, and was not a grant of present and actual Possession; but onely a Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise, That God would give it to him in his own time, and way; which might have been done, though neither <ns0:hi>Iero<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />boam,</ns0:hi> nor the People had used these indirect and evil Cour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses to bring it about; as it befel <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> upon the same oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion.                      </ns0:note> of Israel, to bring the kingdom again to Rehoboam the son of Solo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon.</ns0:p>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Propher, so called; partly, to distinguish him from others of that Name. See <ns0:hi>Nehem.</ns0:hi> 6. 10. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 29. 31. And partly, to add the more weight to his words.</ns0:note>, saying,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 Speak unto Rehoboam the son of Solomon king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah, and Benjamin, and to the remnant of the people, saying,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 Thus saith the LORD, Ye shall not go up nor fight against your brethren the children of Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael: return every man to his house, for this thing is from me <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This event is from my Counsel and Providence, to pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nish <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s Apostacy, though they procured it by sinful means: and therefore, if you proceed, you must fight with me, as well as them.</ns0:note>.                         <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He repaired, and enlarged, and fortified it; for it had been ruined long since; <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 9. 45.                   <ns0:p n="26">26 And Jeroboam said in his heart <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Reasoned within himself. The Phrase discovers the Fountain of his Error, That he did not consult with God, who had given him the Kingdom; as in all reason, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ustice, and gratitude he should have done: nor believed God's Promise, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 11. 38. but his own imaginations, and carnal policies.</ns0:note>, Now shall the kingdom return to the house of David:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 If these people go up to do sacrifice in the house of the LORD at Jerusalem, then shall the heart of this people turn again unto their LORD <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which in it self might seem a prudent conjecture; for this would give <ns0:hi>Rehoboam,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Priests,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Levites,</ns0:hi> the sure and faithful friends of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s House, many op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />portunities of alienating their minds from him, and of re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ducing them to their former Allegiance. But considering God's Providence, by which the hearts of all Men, and the affairs of all Kings and Kingdoms are governed, and of which he had lately seen so eminent an Instance; it was a foolish, as well as wicked course.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> unto Rehoboam king of Judah, and they shall kill me, and go again to Rehoboam king of Judah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves <ns0:hi>of</ns0:hi> gold <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">In imitation of <ns0:hi>Aaron</ns0:hi>'s Golden Calf, and of the <ns0:hi>Egyp<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tians,</ns0:hi> from whom he was lately come. And this he the rather presumed to do, because he knew the people of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> were generally very prone to Superstition, and Idolatry, as their whole History sheweth: and that <ns0:hi>Solomon</ns0:hi>'s example and countenance given to false Worships, had exceedingly strengthned those inclinations; and therefore they were in a great measure prepared for such an Attempt; especially, when his Proposition tended to their own ease, and safety, and profit, which he knew was much dearer to them, as well as to himself, than their Religion.</ns0:note>, and said unto them, It is too much for you <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Too great a trouble and charge, and neither necessary, nor safe for them, as things now stood.</ns0:note> to go up to Jerusalem: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 32. 8.</ns0:note> behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not as if he did himself be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve, or thought to persuade the people to believe, That these Calves were properly, and truly, that very God of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> who brought them out of <ns0:hi>Egypt:</ns0:hi> (which was so mon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strously absurd and ridiculous, that no <ns0:hi>Israelite</ns0:hi> in his right wits could believe it) and had been so far from attaining his end, and satisfying his people, that this would have made him both hateful, and contemptible to them; but his mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing was, that these Images were visible Representations, in, and by which he designed to Worship the True God of <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael,</ns0:hi> as appears, partly from that Parallel-place, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 32. 4. where see my notes: partly, because the Priests and Worshippers of the Calves, are said to Worship <ns0:hi>Iehovah;</ns0:hi> and upon that account, are distinguished from those belong<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to <ns0:hi>Baal;</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 18. 21. and 22. 6, 7. And partly, from <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi>'s design in this Work, which was to quiet the peoples minds, and remove their scruples about going to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> to Worship their God in that place, as they were commanded: which he doth, by signifying to them, That he did not intend any alteration in the substance of their Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ligion; nor to draw them from the Worship of the True God, to the Worship of <ns0:hi>Ashteroth,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Milcom,</ns0:hi> or any of those <ns0:hi>Baals,</ns0:hi> which were set up by <ns0:hi>Solomon;</ns0:hi> but to Wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship that self-same God whom they Worshipped in <ns0:hi>Ierusa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lem,</ns0:hi> even the True God, and the God of their Fathers, who brought them out of <ns0:hi>Egypt;</ns0:hi> but onely to vary a circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stance: and that as they Worshipped God at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> by, and before one Visible Sign, even the Ark, and the Sacred Cherubims there; so his Subjects should Worship God by another Visible Sign, even that of the Calves, in other pla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces; and as for the change of the place, he might suggest to them, that God was present in all places, where Men with honest minds did call upon him; that before the Temple was built, the best of Kings, and Prophets, and People, did Pray, and Sacrifice to God in divers High-places, without any scruple; notwithstanding that restraint of God to one place, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 12. 5, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> That God would dispence with them also in that matter; because going to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> was very dangerous to them at this time; and God would have Mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy, rather than Sacrifice; and God had been pleased to dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pense with his own Ordinances in cases of necessity or great inconvenience, as he did with Circumcision for 40 years in the Wilderness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And he set the one in Bethel, and the other put he in Dan <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Which two places he chose for his peoples convenien<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy; <ns0:hi>Bethel</ns0:hi> being in the <ns0:hi>Southern,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Dan</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>Northern</ns0:hi> parts of his Kingdom.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And this thing became a sin <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> A cause or occasion of great wickedness among that People; not onely of Idolatry, which is called <ns0:hi>Sin</ns0:hi> by way of Eminency; not onely of the Worship of the Calves, wherein they pretended to worship the True God; but also of the Worship of <ns0:hi>Baal,</ns0:hi> and of the utter desertion of the True God; and of all sorts of impiety, and abominable Sins; as is manifest from the History of that Kingdom: in which, there was not one good King: and very few of the people who were not guilty of hainous Crimes, as the Prophets witness.</ns0:note>: for the people went <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The Kings Counsel and Example seduced them, though it did not excuse their Sin; and <ns0:hi>they willingly walked after</ns0:hi> this his wicked <ns0:hi>commandment,</ns0:hi> Hos. 5. 11.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>to worship</ns0:hi> before the one, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> of the Calves.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> unto Dan <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Which is not here mentioned exclusively, for that they went also to <ns0:hi>Bethel</ns0:hi> is evident from <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 32, 33. but for other reasons, either because that of <ns0:hi>Dan</ns0:hi> was first made, or best frequented, the people in those parts having been long leavened with Ido<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />latry: See <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 18. 30. or to shew the peoples readiness to comply with the King's Command, and their Zeal for Idols; that those who lived in, or near <ns0:hi>Bethel,</ns0:hi> had not patience to stay till that Calf was finished, but all of them were forward to go as far as <ns0:hi>Dan,</ns0:hi> which was in the utmost borders of the Land, to Worship an Idol there; when it was thought too much for them to go to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> to Worship God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And he made an house of high places <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>an house (i. e.</ns0:hi> Houses, or Chappels) <ns0:hi>in the high-places.</ns0:hi> Besides the famous Houses, or Temples, which he Built at <ns0:hi>Dan</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Bethel;</ns0:hi> he Built also for his Peoples better accommoda<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, lesser Temples upon divers high-places, which were esteemed Sacred and Venerable, because their Pious An<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cestors had served God in them: and thereby <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi> might not seem to bring in a new Religion, but onely to revive the old.</ns0:note>, and made priests of <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tremities.</ns0:note> the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13. 33. Ezek. 44. 7, 8.</ns0:note> lowest of the people <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Which he might do, either 1. Because the better sort refused it, as an office below their quality: or, 2. Because such would be satisfied with mean allowances; and so he could put into his own Purse a great part of the rich Possessions and Revenues of the <ns0:hi>Levites,</ns0:hi> which doubtless he seized upon when they forsook him, and went to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem;</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 11. 13, 14. which also was very necessary for his present and pressing Occasions; the rather, because he durst not yet lay grievous Taxes upon that People who had new<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly cast off <ns0:hi>Rehoboam</ns0:hi> for that very Reason. Or, 3. Because mean persons would depend upon his favour, and therefore be very pliable to his humour, and firm to his Interest, and zealous to promote the Worship of the Calves. But the Words in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> properly signifie, <ns0:hi>from the ends of the people;</ns0:hi> which is, and may be Translated thus, <ns0:hi>out of all the people;</ns0:hi> promiscuously out of every Tribe.                   <ns0:p n="32">32 And Jeroboam ordained a feast <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either, 1. A Feast of Dedication, like that which was in <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> at the Dedication of the Temple. Or rather, 2. But on the <ns0:hi>15th</ns0:hi> day of the Eighth Month. And this alteration he made, either 1. Or, 3.                         <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> was.</ns0:note> in Judah <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He took his Pattern thence, to shew, That he Worshipped the same God, and Professed the same Religion for substance, which they did; howsoever he diffe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red in circumstances, as here he did in the time.</ns0:note>, and he <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">

                     </ns0:note> offered <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either, 1. By his Priests. Or, rather 2.
